loreChunks.title: A Princess's Temple to Two Gods
loreChunks.text: The Hari Shankar temple in Patan Durbar Square is dedicated to Hari Shankar, a combined form of Vishnu, known as Hari, and Shiva, known as Shankar. It is usually attributed to the early eighteenth century and to Yogamati, a daughter of King Yoganarendra Malla, whose gilded statue on a column stands nearby, though the exact date and circumstances of its founding should be confirmed from inscriptions. Royal women played an important role in temple patronage in Malla Patan, and the temple's dedication to a unified form of Vishnu and Shiva reflects the inclusive religious outlook of the court. The temple collapsed in the 2015 earthquake and was rebuilt in the following years, restoring its place in the row of temples facing the palace. Its history thus spans the final decades of the Malla kingdom and the recovery of Patan's heritage in the twenty-first century.

loreChunks.title: Three Roofs Rebuilt
loreChunks.text: Hari Shankar is a three-tiered Newar pagoda raised on a stepped plinth, with carved roof struts, wooden doors and stone lions on its steps. Its proportions follow the classic form of the square's larger temples, rising in three diminishing roofs crowned by a gilded finial. When it collapsed in 2015, its carved elements were recovered from the rubble where possible, and reconstruction by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust with local craftsmen used traditional joinery, matching timbers and newly carved replacements for pieces that could not be saved. Discreet structural improvements were incorporated to help the temple resist future earthquakes. The contrast between the fresh timber of the rebuilt temple and the darker wood of its neighbours tells the story of 2015 clearly. The project became one of the showcase reconstructions of Patan's post-earthquake recovery and trained many young craftsmen.

loreChunks.title: Vishnu and Shiva United
loreChunks.text: Hari Shankar, also called Harihara, represents the union of Vishnu and Shiva in a single deity, typically shown with one half of the body bearing Vishnu's attributes and the other half Shiva's. The image expresses the idea that the preserver and the destroyer are two aspects of one ultimate reality, a theme that resonates strongly in the Kathmandu Valley, where devotees of different gods share temples and festivals. The temple's struts are noted for scenes depicting the torments of the underworld, reminders of the consequences of wrongdoing and of the god's power to save devotees from suffering. Such imagery, unusual among the square's temples, adds a moral dimension to the building. Visitors who look closely at the struts, original and newly carved, can follow these scenes and compare them with the deities and erotic panels found on other temples in the square.

loreChunks.title: Worship in the Temple Row
loreChunks.text: Hari Shankar receives daily worship from Patan's residents, who include it in their morning rounds of the square's temples. Devotees of both Vishnu and Shiva honour the combined deity, and festivals of both gods bring worshippers, including Ekadashi days sacred to Vishnu and Maha Shivaratri. The temple's reconsecration after its reconstruction was marked by elaborate rituals involving priests, guthi members and residents, who regarded the rebuilding as the restoration of a living shrine rather than simply a monument. During Patan's great festivals, the temple's plinth becomes a viewing platform for processions and crowds. Visitors are welcome to observe from the steps, but should respect worshippers and the sanctum. A guide can explain the meaning of the Hari Shankar image and point out the differences between the original carvings and the new pieces made by today's craftsmen.

loreChunks.title: A Showcase of Post-2015 Rebuilding
loreChunks.text: The reconstruction of Hari Shankar after its collapse in 2015 is one of the best-documented heritage recovery projects in Patan. The Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust, working with the Department of Archaeology and the community, recorded the fallen elements, conserved those that could be reused and commissioned new carvings from local woodcarvers, using historical photographs to guide the work. The project demonstrated that traditional techniques can be combined with modern engineering to improve earthquake resistance without changing a temple's appearance. It also provided training and employment for craftsmen, helping to sustain the skills on which the valley's heritage depends. The rebuilt temple was completed in the years following the earthquake and returned to worship. Visitors can see the results in the crisp new carvings. Field collectors are asked to photograph old and new struts side by side for the record.

audioHook.script: This three-roofed temple looks brand new, and in a way it is. Hari Shankar collapsed completely in the 2015 earthquake, and craftsmen rebuilt it piece by piece, rescuing old carvings from the rubble and carving new ones by hand. The temple honours Hari Shankar, a single god who is half Vishnu and half Shiva, proof that in this valley even the great gods share. Tradition links its founding to Yogamati, a daughter of King Yoganarendra Malla, whose golden statue on the column is just steps away. Look up at the struts: some show the torments of the underworld, a warning carved in wood. Can you tell which carvings survived the earthquake and which were made by today's carvers? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide introduce you to the craftsmen who rebuilt it.

loreChunks.title: One of Patan's Oldest Monasteries
loreChunks.text: Rudra Varna Mahavihar, known locally as Uku Bahal, is regarded as one of the oldest Buddhist monasteries in Patan, located a short walk south of Durbar Square near Mahabouddha. Tradition attributes an early foundation to the site, and the monastery is said to have served as a place of coronation or royal ritual in some periods, though these claims should be confirmed from published surveys and inscriptions. Like other Newar Buddhist monasteries, it is maintained by a sangha of Shakya and Vajracharya families who inherit membership. Over the centuries, donors filled its courtyard with statues and ritual objects, and the present buildings combine Malla-era structures with later additions, including a facade decorated in stucco during the Rana period. The monastery's rich collection of metal sculpture makes it one of the most remarkable courtyards in the valley, yet it receives far fewer visitors than the Golden Temple.

loreChunks.title: A Courtyard of Metal Animals
loreChunks.text: Uku Bahal's courtyard is famous for the dense collection of metal and stone figures that fill its open space: elephants, lions, peacocks, garudas and other creatures, along with statues of donors and royal figures, many mounted on pedestals and some protected by railings. The main shrine faces the courtyard, its facade combining traditional Newar woodwork with stucco decoration added in a later period, which gives the building an unusual appearance among Patan's monasteries. The surrounding wings follow the quadrangular plan typical of Newar monasteries, with rooms for the sangha and for ritual use. Bells, lamps and offerings add to the courtyard's richness. The quality of the metalwork reflects Patan's renown as a centre of bronze casting. Field collectors are asked to photograph the courtyard systematically, recording each sculpture's position, since the collection is vulnerable to theft.

loreChunks.title: Guardians and Donors
loreChunks.text: The animals in Uku Bahal's courtyard carry layered meanings. Elephants and lions are royal symbols of strength and protection, peacocks evoke beauty and the transformation of poison into wisdom, and garudas recall the swift power of the enlightened mind. Many of the figures were donated by devotees as acts of merit, and some bear inscriptions recording the donors' names and dates, which make the courtyard a historical archive as well as a sacred space. The statues of donors and royal figures show how lay patrons placed themselves in perpetual devotion before the Buddha, a practice also seen in the royal columns of the Durbar Squares. The main shrine houses images of the Buddha, honoured daily by the sangha. For visitors, the courtyard offers a vivid lesson in how Buddhist devotion, artistic patronage and community memory combine in a single place.

loreChunks.title: Daily Rituals of the Sangha
loreChunks.text: Uku Bahal remains an active monastery, with daily rituals performed by members of its sangha, who light lamps, make offerings and maintain the shrine. During the Newar Buddhist month of Gunla, devotees visit the monastery regularly, playing traditional music and reciting texts, and the courtyard fills with activity. Major Buddhist festivals, such as Buddha Jayanti, are also celebrated, and the monastery takes part in Patan's wider Buddhist festival calendar. Life-cycle rituals, such as the initiation of young boys into the sangha, are performed here. Visitors are welcome to enter the courtyard quietly, walk clockwise around the shrine and admire the sculptures, but they should not touch the figures, climb on pedestals or photograph rituals without permission. A local guide can explain the meanings of the animals and introduce visitors to the monastery's history and community.

loreChunks.title: Protecting a Sculpture Courtyard
loreChunks.text: Uku Bahal's open courtyard full of metal sculpture makes it particularly vulnerable to theft, and in past decades valuable images have been stolen from monasteries across the valley. Railings and supervision help to protect the figures, but detailed documentation is essential for identifying objects if they disappear. The 2015 earthquake damaged buildings in Patan, and the monastery's structures were inspected and repaired where needed. Metal sculptures exposed to the weather require cleaning and treatment to prevent corrosion, and the stucco facade needs periodic repair. Conservation is the responsibility of the sangha, supported by heritage authorities and donors. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the courtyard and each sculpture from multiple angles, recording positions and any inscriptions, with the sangha's permission, building a record that supports both conservation and protection against theft.

audioHook.script: Step into this quiet courtyard south of Durbar Square and you will find yourself surrounded by a menagerie of metal: elephants, lions, peacocks and garudas, standing on pedestals among statues of kneeling donors. This is Uku Bahal, the Rudra Varna Mahavihar, regarded as one of the oldest Buddhist monasteries in Patan. Every animal here was a gift, offered by families hoping to earn merit, and some still carry the donors' names. Few visitors find their way here, compared with the Golden Temple, so you may have the courtyard almost to yourself. Look at the shrine's facade too: Newar woodwork meets later stucco decoration. Can you find the garuda among the animals? Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a Patan guide tell you the stories behind the statues.
